title: Food packaging and bisphenol A and bis(2-ethyhexyl) phthalate exposure: findings from a dietary intervention
authors: Rudel RA, Gray JM, Engel CL, Rawsthorne TW, Dodson RE, Ackerman JM, et al.
followUp: 8 days: usual diet, 3 days of fresh foods, usual diet
population: Five families, 10 adults and 10 children, in the San Francisco Bay Area selected for frequent consumption of canned and packaged foods
funder: This research was supported by the Passport Foundation (Charlotte, NC, USA) and the Susan S. Bailis Breast Cancer Research Fund at Silent Spring Institute.
authorConflicts: Four authors are employed by Silent Spring Institute, a public charity; three by the Breast Cancer Fund, which advocates stricter regulation of chemicals including bisphenol A; one by AXYS Analytical Services Ltd, an analytical chemistry laboratory. The authors declare no competing financial interests.
result: Uncontrolled before-after intervention. During 3 days of fresh foods not canned or packaged in plastic, geometric mean urinary bisphenol A fell from 3.7 to 1.2 ng/ml (66%) and DEHP metabolites by 53% to 56% (MEHHP 57 to 25 ng/ml); maxima fell by 76% for bisphenol A and 93% to 96% for DEHP metabolites.
